Two freehold Camden Park bungalow plots for sale at $26 mil and $27 mil
article:
Two adjacent freehold sites in the Camden Park Good Class Bungalow (GCB) area are being offered for sale through an expression of interest (EOI) exercise. The residential sites, which each house a single-storey detached bungalow, are located at 15 and 15A Camden Park.

The sites are held under separate titles by the same owner, and are being offered for sale individually, marketing agent CBRE said in a Nov 10 release. Offers may be submitted for either property or for both.

The site at 15 Camden Park spans a land area of 13,116 sq ft and has a guide price of $26 million, or $1,982 psf. The site at 15A Camden Park measures 14,060 sq ft and is priced at $27 million, or $1,920 psf.

Each plot could potentially be redeveloped into “a substantial family residence”, said Rowena Chan, senior vice president of residential capital markets, Singapore at CBRE.

“Their adjoining location also provides an additional option for buyers seeking a larger landholding or wishing to establish neighbouring family homes,” she added.

Subject to prevailing planning requirements, site conditions and relevant approvals, the adjoining titles may be acquired together as a combined 27,176 sq ft holding.

According to CBRE, the properties were formerly the residence of the late Earnest Lau and Kwa Geok Lian.

Located in the Camden Park landed residential enclave in Bukit Timah, the sites are less than 1km from the Singapore Botanic Gardens, while the Botanic Gardens MRT Interchange (serving the Circle and Downtown lines) is also within walking distance.

The Camden Park area has 26 homes, with landholdings in the enclave averaging at approximately 22,605 sq ft, said CBRE.

As such, the properties at 15 and 15A Camden Park each offer “the prestige and privacy of a GCB area address at a more manageable overall investment quantum”, the firm added.

Caveats lodged show that the most recent transaction in Camden Park was for a detached house on a 29,922 sq ft freehold plot that fetched $48 million ($1,604 psf) in November 2025.

Before that, the last transaction occurred in September 2021, when a freehold detached home occupying a 16,607 sq ft site changed hands for $32.5 million ($1,957 psf).

The EOI will close at 5pm on Jan 20, 2027.

title: Tampines Mall completes $24 mil asset enhancement initiative
article:
Tampines Mall is completing its $24 million asset enhancement initiative (AEI) in December, marking a new chapter for the eight-storey shopping centre in the Tampines Regional Centre.

The mall, owned by CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust (CICT), began the AEI in September 2025 to improve about 50,000 sq ft of net lettable area.

In its 3Q2026 financial update, published on Oct 29, CICT said around 97% of the AEI space is committed or in advanced negotiation as of Sept 30.

In a separate Nov 10 release, Tampines Mall said the transformation introduces 21 new brands, including 15 making their debut in the East. The mall now houses over 160 stores, with a net lettable area exceeding 356,000 sq ft.

“The refreshed Tampines Mall brings together a broad mix of premium, accessible-luxury and everyday brands, alongside dining, sports and lifestyle offerings and well-loved favourites,” added Adrian Lai, general manager of Tampines Mall.

A highlight of the revamped mall is a beauty cluster with 14 brands, including Sephora.

The beauty retailer, which previously operated at neighbouring shopping centre Tampines 1 now occupies ground-floor space that was formerly part of Isetan. The Japanese department store closed its Tampines Mall outlet in November 2025 after 30 years.

Other brands in the beauty cluster include new-to-Tampines Mall names such as British skincare brand Elemis, Chinese makeup retailer Judydoll, Dutch home and body cosmetics brand Rituals, as well as luxury brand YSL Beauty.

In addition, beauty brands such as Shiseido and Chanel, which previously operated through store concessions within Isetan, have opened standalone boutiques in the mall.

Another highlight of the AEI is a refresh of the dining line-up at Tampinese Mall. New additions include Italian dining concept Casa Vostra, Chinese milk tea brand Charlie’s Tea, Hong Kong-founded Ging Sun Ho King of Bun and specialty coffee shop Alchemist.

The mall has also expanded its jewellery and fashion offerings. Key changes include Decathlon, which closed their click-and-collect store at Tampines Mall at the start of the year. The French sports retailer is moving into a more spacious 18,000 sq ft store on Level 2 that will open in December.

Other new names include German leather goods store Braun Büffel, international fashion brand Meilleur Moment, watch dealer Vincent Watch and travel accessories store Boarding Gate.

Tampines Mall first opened in 1995. It is adjacent to the Tampines MRT interchange (serving the East-West and Downtown lines) and the Tampines Bus Interchange. It also neighbours two other malls, Century Square and Tampines 1, which are both owned by Frasers Centrepoint Trust.

title: 3 US Stocks Down 30% – Are They Worth a Look?
article:
As tech leaders fall sharply from their peaks, investors are split on what to do next.
Some see it as a long-awaited Wall Street sale to grab a piece of these
tech titans
on the cheap.
Others contemplate a possible value trap.
Three technology leaders –
Alphabet Inc.
(NASDAQ: GOOGL),
Fortinet Inc.
(NASDAQ: FTNT), and
Broadcom Inc.
(NASDAQ: AVGO) – have seen roughly 30% of their equity values wiped out from the recent pullbacks.
Let’s unpack the insights behind their massive stock rout.
Alphabet: Capex Anxiety Meets Cloud Growth
Alphabet’s share price pulled back sharply from its peak of more than US$400 in May 2026 to around US$280, wiping out close to one-third of its market capitalisation.
The catalyst?
Earnings per share (EPS) missed in the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), coming in at US$2.12 against consensus analyst estimates of US$3.02.
As Alphabet owns a stake in the publicly listed SpaceX, a fall in the share price of the latter caused a non-operating accounting loss of US$8.7 billion for the quarter, which weighed on the bottom line.
Furthermore, Alphabet’s heavy capital outlays spooked investors, as it announced 3Q2026 quarterly capex of US$51.4 billion, pushing its free cash flow (FCF) to negative US$9.1 billion.
Although Alphabet’s 2026 capex is expected to stay within the guided range of US$195 billion to US$205 billion, capex spending in 2027 is projected to increase significantly, fuelling investors’ concerns.
However, Alphabet’s operating engines remain strong.
Its 3Q2026 revenue surged 25% year on year (YoY) to US$127.6 billion, driven by Google Cloud, which climbed 103% to US$30.7 billion.
Meanwhile, operating income increased 30% YoY to US$40.58 billion, with the operating margin improving from 31% to 32%, demonstrating improving operating leverage.
Right now, the market is offering Alphabet’s shares at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 13x – a significant discount relative to its
Magnificent Seven
peers, which trade at a median P/E of 31.6x.
Fortinet: Bottom-line Momentum Persists Despite Rising Costs
Fortinet share price has fallen around 30% despite the global cybersecurity company’s 3Q2026 revenue expanding 20% YoY to US$2.08 billion.
The revenue growth was driven by a 37% surge in product revenue to US$765 million, anchored by the growth in secure networking hardware and term licences.
Meanwhile, service revenue grew 13% to US$1.31 billion as the revenue for FortiGuard and other security subscription services was recognised.
Crucially, total gross margin contracted 1.8 percentage points to 79% as Fortinet shifts towards lower-margin product revenue, with the margin compression worsened by rising costs of memory chips and inventory-related expenses.
Moreover, although Fortinet is winning massive enterprise clients, these clients typically activate their services in phases, meaning the revenue is realised more slowly, exerting top-line pressure on Fortinet.
Still, Fortinet’s bottom-line momentum remains strong.
Its 3Q2026 operating income surged 29% to US$704.3 million and it delivered US$864.8 million in FCF. Fortinet demonstrated strong operating leverage as its top-line growth outpaced expense growth.
The verdict?
The latest sell-off reflects short-term market anxieties, rather than a structural decline of Fortinet’s business.
Broadcom: Valuation Reset vs Custom AI Dominance
From a peak of around US$490, Broadcom’s share price has dropped more than 30% to about US$330 per share, resetting its trailing P/E from over 70 to a more palatable level of over 40.
Still, investors should not ignore the custom chip designer’s concentration risk, with direct sales to one distributor accounting for 50% of its 3Q2026 net revenue.
In addition, its top five end customers account for approximately 55% of 3QFY2026 net revenue.
Despite these concentration risks, Broadcom remains dominant in custom chip design.
Revenue for its AI-driven Semiconductor Solutions segment skyrocketed 127% YoY to US$20.8 billion, lifting consolidated 3Q2026 revenue 85.5% YoY to US$29.59 billion, with an operating margin of 53.9%.
Backed by long-term demand from Big Tech firms such as Alphabet, Broadcom’s AI-led growth is expected to continue to 2031.
Crucially, Broadcom’s business is cash generative.
In the nine months ended 2 August 2026 (9MFY2026), Broadcom’s FCF increased 64.2% YoY to $31.9 billion – a stark contrast to hyperscalers alarming negative FCF.
The current valuation reset of a
cash-rich business
like Broadcom may make it worth a closer look for long-term investors.
Get Smart: Navigating Market Declines with Discipline
A 30% contraction is an opportunity, not necessarily to buy, but to analyse the reason behind it with discipline rather than emotions.
It’s easy to succumb to myopic market noise and lose sight of durable businesses that compound in value over time.
Amid market overreactions, Alphabet, Fortinet, and Broadcom display unique strengths.
Has the market bottomed? No one knows.
Smart investors know better than to time the bottom.
Instead, they buy in stages and track the operating metrics that truly matter.
If the market falls further, will you be ready… or fully invested?

title: Anthropic filing snafu jolts investors in run-up to mega IPO
article:
(Nov 10): Anthropic PBC is set to kick off the formal marketing of its blockbuster initial public offering (IPO) as early as Tuesday after an apparent snafu over the filing documents added a dose of last-minute drama to a nervous market.

Monday’s brief clerical misstep, in which a leaked prospectus mistakenly dangled a US$69.3 billion ($88.5 billion) fundraising target before getting retracted, provided an unexpected jolt to investors preparing for the Claude chatbot maker’s offering. The number, which the company reportedly later said was outdated, indicated a target that would fall short of an earlier goal of matching SpaceX’s record-setting debut.

Once the deal kicks off, Anthropic will be in a position to make the case to investors that now is the right time to go public despite last week’s swoon in artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks. The gyrations of the past week briefly sent the Cboe Volatility Index, known as the fear gauge, above 25. That’s a zone in which companies typically postpone their IPOs, said Matt Kennedy, senior strategist at IPO research firm Renaissance Capital.

Anthropic has little time to wait for the market to rediscover its love of AI, if its goal is to go public before the US Thanksgiving holiday on Nov 26. The size of Anthropic’s IPO and its investment case may put it in a different category from the average listing, Kennedy said.

“It’s such a big deal and such a unique asset that if the company wants to move forward, they can,” Kennedy said. “It just becomes a matter of where it prices.”

Anthropic will start marketing its IPO on Tuesday morning, IFR reported, citing people it didn’t identify. A spokesperson for Anthropic declined to comment.

See also: Anthropic IPO buyers see valuation as low as US$1.1 tril

The expected decision to move forward would keep the debate over its valuation target going, after some potential investors discussed a range of about US$1.1 trillion to US$1.3 trillion, Bloomberg News reported Friday. That’s well below where talks had been focused just a month before; in the interim, the Nasdaq 100 Index plunged 14%.

Against that backdrop of heightened market sensitivity adding to the valuation debate, Reuters reported that the company sent out and retracted a filing. Anthropic first sent bankers a copy of a document that indicated a sale of about 867 million shares in a price range of US$70 to US$80 per share, but then followed up with an email saying that those details were inaccurate, Reuters said. An Anthropic spokesperson declined to comment on the errant filing.

See also: Dubai firm raises US$529 mil in UAE’s first IPO of the year

The retracted document was an updated prospectus sent by Anthropic’s outside counsel in Canada, The Information reported, citing people it didn’t identify. The counsel later told the banks that some of the details were inaccurate and it would update the filing later, it said.

Starting formal IPO marketing early this week, immediately following the end of a 15-day waiting period after last month’s public filing, would put the company on track to officially price the offering and debut on the Nasdaq Global Select Market the week of Nov 16.

The effort to win over institutional buyers will kick off immediately, with one-on-one and group meetings between management and investors around the world, either virtually or in person. Retail investors — who may get as much as 20% of the available shares, people familiar with the matter have said — will be tapped from the US to Japan to the UK.

Anthropic will need to quell worries about risks that have loomed larger as its IPO has progressed. Its quarterly revenue growth slowed at the end of the third quarter, and the data centers providing its computing power could be heading for a reckoning as a result of the Democrats’ success in the midterm elections — the trigger for last week’s stock sell-off.

Concern over AI safety is also increasing, and although Anthropic is a major proponent of slowing the development of the most advanced models, AI-sceptic Democrats may push interventions that differ from the company’s preferred solutions.

“Certainly buying shares in a company like this carries risks,” Kennedy said, “but there is also some risk in not owning a company that is disrupting so many other industries”.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Some loss of confidence in the AI trade is not surprising given the shift in political direction after last week’s US midterm election results, said Vivek Seth, chief executive officer of Shaires Holdings Ltd. The London-listed, AI-focused investment company backs Anthropic for its long-term fundamentals, he added.

“Anthropic is a once-in-a-generation company,” Seth said, citing its rapid growth, institutional backing and more than US$130 billion in cash and short-term investments. “Its IPO will establish a market-clearing valuation as conditions stabilise.”

Peter Singlehurst, the head of Baillie Gifford’s private companies team and manager of a fund that already owns a stake in Anthropic, echoed Seth’s praise, calling the company “exceptional” and touting its products’ potential to act more like a collaborator or team member, instead of just helping users work faster.

The biggest opportunity in AI may be in solving the hardest problems, rather than doing the greatest volume of work, Singlehurst explained.

“Some models are cheaper and perfectly good for routine tasks, but customers may pay substantially more for models that can reason better, tackle harder problems and work independently for longer,” he said.

Anthropic’s IPO filings left blank spaces indicating a potential price range, suggesting the company intends to give investors a way to signal their enthusiasm, or their indifference, through more than just their decision of whether to bid. That stands in contrast with SpaceX’s US$86.2 billion IPO in June, which came at a fixed price that left no wiggle room for negotiation with buyers.

Volatility in AI stocks during the marketing could play an outsize role in whether Anthropic investors lob in bids at the top of the range, after the sharp selloff left potential buyers nursing losses in their portfolios and less eager to take on exposure to new stocks, which are typically riskier. Still, some investors see greater risk to their annual returns from not participating in what could be the biggest IPO of all time, and being left behind.

“If Anthropic can take what it has achieved in coding into areas such as law, finance and medical research, where exceptional expertise is also highly valued, the opportunity is enormous,” Singlehurst said.

title: Energy security needs action on electrification — International Renewable Energy Agency
article:
(Nov 10): Wars and energy shocks are accelerating the case to electrify economies as governments seek to curb exposure to volatile fossil-fuel prices and limit imports.

Electricity is increasingly replacing fossil fuels in transport, heating and industry, and nations should aim to accelerate that shift, Francesco La Camera, director general of the International Renewable Energy Agency, said at the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey.

A flagship ambition for the talks is to win commitments to increase electricity’s share of global final energy consumption from just over 20% today to 35% by 2035.

That is “exactly what we have to put into action to keep our promise alive,” La Camera said in an interview Monday. “If we don’t act, we cannot win the challenge of climate change.”

Electrification can reduce reliance on imported fuels, stabilise energy costs and strengthen economic resilience, La Camera said. “Everyone has realised that a centralised system based on fossil fuels is not good for energy security,” he said.

A series of meetings at the summit Tuesday were convening energy ministers, bankers and company executives on the electrification goal.

See also: China set to lead world in energy investment in 2026, CCTV says

“If you succeed in electrification, you’ll reduce dependency and you’ll fight climate change,” Turkey’s Deputy Energy and Natural Resources Minister Zafer Demircan said Monday. The summit host aims to lift electricity’s share of the nation’s final energy consumption to 36% by 2040 from about 22% currently.

Falling costs are strengthening the economic case for renewables, according to Irena. Since 2010, the levelised cost of electricity from solar PV has fallen by 89%, onshore wind by 71%, and offshore wind by 63%, the organisation said in a July report.

Disruption to oil and gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz as a result of the Iran war has also added urgency to the deployment of renewables.

See also: India approves US$1.5 bil push for energy storage capacity

“We’re seeing more and more governments looking at what’s happening in the war and actually seeing that as a catalyst for them to really upscale renewables in their own country,” said Rebecca Williams, deputy CEO of the Global Wind Energy Council, an industry group.

More investment is needed to increase adoption of clean energy, particularly in offshore wind, where upfront costs are high, La Camera said.

Funding for renewables projects remains a constraint, according to Turkey’s Demircan. “The main thing is to find the financing,” he said.

title: New World’s top shareholder seeks bank loan as equity deal looms — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 10): Chow Tai Fook Enterprises Ltd, an investment arm of Hong Kong’s billionaire Cheng family, is seeking about HK$5 billion (US$637 million or $810 million) in fresh funding from banks, according to people familiar with the matter.

The financing would be a new-money loan and would be used for general corporate purposes, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private matters.

The fundraising would provide CTFE, New World Development Co’s largest shareholder, with a liquidity cushion if it decides to proceed with a broad recapitalisation of the cash-strapped builder. Such a move could include a rights issue, a mechanism where existing stockholders can buy new shares in proportion to their current holdings, other people familiar with the matter said last month.

The potential new loan for CTFE could be signed as soon as this month, though details are still under discussion, the people said.

CTFE and New World didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

The Chengs have been floating capital injection proposals for months as they explore options to support New World. That’s kept investors focused on how CTFE could raise cash to back any transaction.

See also: Hong Kong bourse operator's profit falls as AI scrutiny hits listings, trading

New World is still reeling from the property downturn in mainland China and Hong Kong and reported a HK$19.7 billion (US$2.5 billion) net loss for its latest fiscal year.

The builder has been seeking approval from its bank lenders to extend by two years about HK$88 billion in loans, which were secured in Hong Kong’s largest ever debt refinancing in 2025.

See also: Hong Kong chip IPOs tap intertwined networks of investors and bosses

The company plans to repay 10% of the loan principal using proceeds from the equity injection, which it aims to complete by January.

If a rights issue does go through, it would represent a major sign of direct financial backing from the controlling family for the debt-laden company. The developer has a market capitalisation of about HK$12.8 billion as of Nov 10, down 88% from its peak in 2019.

title: Vodafone raises profit forecast after cost cutting campaign
article:
(Nov 10): Vodafone Group Plc raised its full-year profit guidance after the British phone company cut costs and the size of its workforce.

Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation after leases will rise to €13.2 billion (US$14.8 billion) to €13.4 billion for the fiscal year ending in March, the company said in a statement on Tuesday. That compares to the €13 billion to €13.3 billion range Vodafone had forecast in July.

Chief executive officer Margherita Della Valle has been selling assets and reducing costs, which included cutting more than 3,000 jobs across Europe in the first half, to try to reignite growth at telecom company. Most of the company’s growth comes from less saturated markets in Africa and the Middle East, while its largest units in Europe face heavy competition for subscribers.

The company said it delivered €700 million in annual gross savings between 2023 and 2026 due to staff cuts and other measures. It expects to reduce European operating expenditures by over €200 million in the 2027 fiscal year and has announced 2,300 role reductions in Germany.

Vodafone’s shares closed at 116.95 pence on Monday and have gained 18% this year.

In the UK, the company combined with CK Hutchison Holdings Ltd’s rival business Three, taking the number of large mobile operators to three from four. Vodafone took full control of the venture earlier this year, and Della Valle said the merged business would save £1 billion ($1.3 billion) annually by 2032. The extra savings will come from shutting down overlapping sites and upgrading the two networks to be more efficient, the company said last month.

See also: Infineon boosts AI sales outlook due to data centre growth plans

The company is recovering from a 2024 law change in the German market that barred landlords from bundling rent with TV and broadband services, costing the company millions of customers. Vodafone is using broadband connections to differentiate from some competitors by selling bundles with mobile services.

title: Deeper economic slump tests Marcos, Philippine Central Bank
article:
(Nov 10): A surprise slowdown in the Philippine economy has triggered calls for the central bank to go easy on interest rate increases and for Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr to do more to revive growth.

Economists from China Banking Corporation, Metropolitan Bank & Trust Co, Union Bank of the Philippines and Pantheon Macroeconomics have raised the possibility that the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas will pause its rate hikes after economic growth last quarter decelerated to the weakest since the pandemic.

“It sure doesn’t make much sense to slam hard on the brakes if we’re driving uphill on rocky terrain,” Metropolitan Bank chief economist Nicholas Mapa said.

Resurgent inflation due to the protracted Iran war and farm damage from monsoon rains have further strained the consumption-driven, import-dependent economy that is already falling behind most of its Southeast Asian neighbours. Household spending, a key economic pillar, remained tepid and weighed on a swathe of industries from retail to real estate.

Reacting to the poor data, Marcos’ office on Tuesday (Nov 10) said it is working to stabilise prices of basic goods and ensure a sufficient supply of food and fuel. “We are doing everything we can. The government is not neglecting its duties,” his press officer Claire Castro said at a briefing.

See also: Canada expands US tariff exemptions, cuts some aluminium relief

The central bank has said fiscal measures are expected to help the economy recover after it surprised markets with an outsized half-point increase last month. Governor Eli Remolona last week said the BSP remains in a tightening cycle as it fights persistent price pressures.

Inflation accelerated to a higher-than-expected 7.8% in October, well above its 3% target, and Remolona last week said it will take “a few more months” to peak.

The growth outlook for this quarter, meanwhile, remains gloomy, despite a typical consumption boost during the Christmas holidays. El Niño, which alters rainfall patterns and can fuel drought, is threatening to inflict more pain on the agriculture sector, which already suffered a record slump last quarter.

See also: Vietnam turns to taxes, state borrowing to finance growth push

“Looking ahead, economic growth is likely to remain subdued through the fourth quarter before recovering toward the 4%–5% range by the first quarter of 2027,” said Domini Velasquez, chief economist at Manila-based China Banking. “Demand conditions remain clearly weak, with a sizable negative output gap.”

But Bloomberg Economics and Bank of America said the BSP is likely to stay on course with its monetary tightening cycle despite weaker growth, with looming risks to inflation including El Niño.

Complicating any shift in the central bank’s tightening policy is the peso, which has declined almost 7% this year to be Asia’s second-worst-performing currency against the dollar. The peso strengthened 0.65% on Tuesday, recovering losses from the previous day and moving in line with gains in other regional currencies.

With weak economic growth constraining the central bank’s room for rate increases, the government “must do the heavy lifting", according to Jonathan Ravelas, a senior adviser at Reyes Tacandong & Co in Manila. Officials should, in particular, increase food supply by rebuilding local production to lower prices, he said.

The worsening economic slump has also prompted businesses to call on the Marcos administration to act. The Makati Business Club — which counts senior executives of the nation’s biggest companies as members — said the government should continue to restore business confidence and accelerate infrastructure projects.

“The policy response must go beyond stimulating economic activity and attracting investments,” MBC executive director Julia Abad said in a statement. “It must strengthen governance, institutions and policy execution.”

title: Infineon boosts AI sales outlook due to data centre growth plans
article:
(Nov 10): Infineon Technologies AG raised its 2027 data centre sales forecast, signalling confidence that the business will drive growth even as investor concerns mount over the artificial intelligence boom.

The German chipmaker sees data centre sales growing to around €4 billion (US$4.5 billion) in the year that ends in September, it said in a statement on Tuesday. Previously, Infineon forecast AI data centre power solutions would make €2.5 billion in the period. It also makes about €500 million annually from traditional data centres, and the new figure comprises both segments.

“We expect a significant increase in revenue and profitability in fiscal year 2027,” chief executive officer Jochen Hanebeck said in the statement, adding power chips for data centres and electromobility would be among the growth drivers.

Concerns about a possible AI bubble have driven a steep selloff in companies from chipmakers to so-called neoclouds. Infineon’s shares have declined by 45% from a peak in June. Demand for data centre chips has helped Infineon and peers such as STMicroelectronics NV compensate for slow revenue recovery from the struggling automotive sector.

Infineon is the only one among European chipmakers to give a full year forecast. The company tends to guide cautiously and then adjust estimates as visibility improves, according to JPMorgan analysts including Sandeep Deshpande. JPMorgan had expected Infineon to guide for 2027 data center revenue, including CPU and other non-AI accelerator-related power revenue, of between €3.5 billion and €4 billion.

As the buildout of data centers around the world accelerated, demand for Infineon’s chips to control power soared. Those chips can support advanced processors such as those from Nvidia Corp that are fuelling the AI boom.

See also: Zara owner backs new fund targeting supply chain emissions

However, a punishing post-US election selloff has rippled across the industry. Some potential investors in Anthropic PBC, which can begin formal marketing of its initial public offering as soon as Tuesday, discussed a valuation ranging from about US$1.1 trillion to US$1.3 trillion, well below where talks had been focused just a month ago, Bloomberg News reported last week.

Infineon’s fiscal 2026 revenue was €16.35 billion, matching analysts’ estimates, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The company sees sales growing to about €20 billion in the current year. The board will propose increasing the 2026 dividend by three cents to €0.38.

Infineon said its adjusted gross margin will be in the mid-to-high forties percentage range in the period and it plans investments of €3 billion to €3.5 billion. Adjusted gross margin was 43.1% in fiscal 2026.

See also: Vodacom profit jumps 26% as Safaricom gains boost earnings

The main areas of investment will be equipment for the ramp-up of production at Infineon’s Dresden site in Germany, the expansion of silicon carbide capacities in Malaysia, and the start of gallium nitride manufacturing on 300-millimetre wafers in the Austrian town of Villach.

Infineon is also considering setting up wafer fabrication in Thailand, although such a move is unlikely in the next three years. In September, Infineon announced it will sell parts of its memory business to focus on its core activities and more dynamic parts of its portfolio.

title: FWD Private issues US$318 million insurance policy
article:
On Nov 10, FWD Private (Bermuda) announced that it has achieved a new GUINNESS WORLD RECORDS™ title for the most valuable life insurance policy. Valued at US$318 million (issued in Hong Kong), the policy issued by FWD Private provides a tailored, comprehensive solution that supports an individual customer’s wealth preservation and intergenerational legacy planning.

Established in 2023, FWD Private offers comprehensive legacy planning solutions and services for high-net-worth (HNW) and ultra-high-net-worth (UHNW) individuals.

Shelyne Shum, Chief Partnership Distribution Officer, FWD Private, said, "This record-breaking policy marks an important milestone for FWD and reflects the trust that HNW customers place in us. It further reinforces FWD’s leadership in the HNW segment and demonstrates our proven capabilities across wealth and legacy planning and protection strategies. Building on our strong foundation, FWD Private continues to accelerate growth across Asia and deliver tailored legacy planning solutions that empower customers and their families to truly celebrate living.”

She added, "A case of this scale and complexity calls for tremendous collaboration. My heartfelt thanks go to our external partners, including broker adviser Charles Monat Associates, private bank and reinsurers, as well as internal teams across distribution, case management, product solutions, underwriting and corporate governance, for their dedication and collective effort in delivering this remarkable policy. This achievement is also a testament to the strength of our distribution network and the deep partnerships we have built across the industry.”

Teddy Chu, Chief Executive Officer, Hong Kong, Charles Monat Associates, said, “We are incredibly proud to contribute to this new GUINNESS WORLD RECORDS™ title of the most valuable life insurance policy for the second consecutive time, led by the same Charles Monat Associates consultant. Our track record and experience in advising clients on complex solutions has played a key role in supporting the appropriate legacy solution for this remarkable case. This new record policy underscores Hong Kong's position as one of the world's leading wealth management and life insurance hub, reinforcing the importance of collaboration among brokers, insurers, and bank partners to address the evolving wealth planning needs of HNW and UHNW individuals.”

title: Insurers react to riot risks across Europe by capping coverage
article:
(Nov 10): Insurers are taking steps to limit their exposure to the risk of losses tied to a wave of street protests in cities across Europe.

The industry has started imposing caps on coverage, raising deductibles and — in some high-risk locations — eliminating coverage altogether, according to Marcos Alvarez, who oversees global insurance at Morningstar DBRS.

Such risks, which fall into the insurance category of strikes, riots and civil commotion (SRCC), have been on the rise in Europe in recent years. And according to Allianz SE, Europe’s biggest insurer, companies increasingly need to treat SRCC as a risk not just associated with emerging markets but also with high-income countries.

The development has been on full display across the continent in recent weeks, as student protests that started in France morphed into region-wide demonstrations centred on a wide range of basic affordability issues. Anger over planned data centres is also leading to protests. As civil unrest continues, industry insiders are starting to draw parallels between SRCC risks and the kind of damage that’s normally associated with natural disasters like hurricanes, Alvarez said.

“Because of the severity and the magnitude of losses, SRCC is now behaving like a natural catastrophe,” he said. “These aren’t secondary threats anymore.”

Nicolas Aubert, CEO of Howden France, says the changing face of SRCC is now “actively reshaping” coverage terms.

See also: Thailand shifts disaster risk to insurers with US$467 mil plan

“Insurers have had to move quickly to speed up claims payments and support affected businesses,” he said. “The strain shows in tighter terms — higher deductibles, lower limits and coverage restrictions", all of which is “leaving some policyholders exposed".

More than half a million people took part in marches across France in mid-October, with violence and looting disrupting demonstrations and damaging public buildings and stores. Since then, police dramatically stepped up their presence and requirements were introduced in an effort to keep marches free of violence. Protests have also gripped cities in Germany, Belgium and Portugal as affordability issues fuel widespread discontent.

Ian Humphries, who heads Allianz’s political violence and terrorism unit in London, says the insurer isn’t applying “any broad reactive restrictions” based on the latest protests. Instead, coverage is done on a “case-by-case underwriting basis” and takes into account factors such as “proximity to areas that may be more susceptible to civil unrest", he said.

See also: Great Eastern investing in Granite Private Credit Fund — Bloomberg

The insurance industry has sought to keep up with the rise in SRCC risks by developing tools to help measure the new landscape. In September, Howden launched an analytics programme called UNREST to give insurers and reinsurers access to more recent data on the impact of strikes, riots and civil unrest.

Howden says its model helps insurers identify where exposures are concentrated, how events might unfold and the potential portfolio impacts. SRCC threats are becoming more frequent and localised, and older models don’t adequately capture the real risks insurers now face, the broker said.

While SRCC coverage has historically been offered as a standard part of commercial policies, insurers are now treating such risks separately to reflect the potential for significant losses, according to AM Best, a credit-rating firm specialised in the insurance industry.

“As evidenced by multibillion-dollar losses from the unrest in Minneapolis and New Caledonia in 2020 and 2024, the 2025 Nepal riots, and the recent widespread destruction in France, SRCC events can have a significant impact,” Mathilde Jakobsen, senior director at AM Best, said in a recent note.

Protests in France have so far disproportionately affected commercial premises and public buildings, with insured losses expected to be below €1.2 billion to cover, according to Morningstar DBRS. The figure may yet be revised higher if the unrest continues.

“Typical riots were concentrated in one city for a couple of days, but now the violence is being correlated across a country or even across several countries,” Alvarez said. “When you have losses from lots of properties at the same time, that puts a different type of strain on insurers’ capital, earnings and capital ratios.”

Verisk Maplecroft, which models SRCC catastrophe risk, describes the protests in Europe as the “most significant concurrent unrest” seen in the region in years. Verisk’s risk gauge for large-scale unrest in Europe is currently at its highest since 2021.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

“Large demonstrations do not inevitably descend into rioting or looting, but the pattern seen in recent weeks — whereby initially peaceful protests have at times been joined or exploited by more confrontational groups — means that further damaging unrest cannot be ruled out,” said Jess Middleton, senior Europe analyst at Verisk Maplecroft.

Such risks aren’t new in France, though the economic loss has been rising in recent years. The Gilets Jaunes protests of 2018-19 resulted in about €220 million in insured losses, according to Morningstar. The riots of June 2023 generated some €730 million in insured losses. It is not yet clear what the latest protests will end up costing.

The unrest has “prompted further discussions around the need for French government reinsurance solutions to cover future SRCC events", Humphries of Allianz said.

France this year approved the creation of a state-backed fund to provide mandatory riot coverage in property policies for all businesses and homeowners across the country. The fund is expected to go into effect in January and will be financed by contributions levied on insurers, as well as a 0.8% increase in premiums paid by policyholders, Alvarez says. Insurers will retain 10% of the loss exposure.

“It ensures they still have skin in the game,” he said.

title: Chinese coal buyers balk at Indonesian miners’ contract demands
article:
(Nov 10): Chinese coal buyers are pushing back against attempts by some Indonesian miners to rewrite 2027 supply contracts in ways that would shift the risk of government-driven disruptions onto customers, threatening to delay deals that underpin decisions on output.

Some Indonesian producers are seeking waiver clauses that would release them from obligations to deliver contracted volumes if Jakarta cuts output quotas or delays export approvals, according to people with knowledge of the matter. Chinese buyers are reluctant to accept such provisions, particularly after changes in government policy contributed to disruptions in deliveries this year, said the people, asking not to be named discussing confidential contract terms.

Indonesia, the world’s biggest exporter of thermal coal, is exerting greater control over output and exports of the fossil fuel to safeguard supplies for domestic power production. Miners must meet local obligations before they can go ahead with overseas sales while the government is also routing exports through state-controlled channels to improve pricing transparency and curb practices such as under-invoicing.

As a result, Indonesian coal exports to China are down almost 10% in the first 10 months from a year earlier, according to data from Kpler. That’s even as overall production is forecast to be around 720 million tonnes this year, ahead of the government’s initial target of 600 million tonnes.

The changes in Indonesia, under the so-called RKAB work plan and budget system that seeks to control mining production volumes, are complicating negotiations with customers.

Some Chinese traders are delaying annual contract talks as they wait for greater clarity on Jakarta’s production target and the allocation of individual mining quotas, according to analysts who cover the sector, asking not to be named due to the sensitivity of the matter. Further delays could mean that producers enter the new year without certainty over how much coal they are authorised to mine.

See also: US seeks deeper Myanmar ties, access to ‘bountiful’ rare earths

The policy shifts may be more disruptive for contracts with overseas customers than production. Indonesia will probably keep output at about 700 million tonnes next year, so an export supply squeeze is unlikely, said Glen Kurokawa, an analyst at CRU Group.

Delayed contracts and broad waiver clauses could leave individual Chinese buyers uncertain whether nominated supplies will be delivered, however. That could increase their exposure to spot-price volatility and potentially push demand toward Indonesia’s competitors including Australia and Mongolia.

title: Zara owner backs new fund targeting supply chain emissions
article:
(Nov 10): Inditex SA is backing a fund set up to grant low-cost loans to suppliers that invest in energy efficiency, as the fashion industry faces pressure to cut its carbon footprint.

In a private-public partnership that chief executive officer Óscar García Maceiras says is the first of its kind, the world’s biggest fashion retailer has committed US$50 million to the fund, which is led by the International Finance Corporation, the World Bank’s private-sector arm. IFC plans to raise US$400 million to help small companies transition to net-zero business models.

As much as 8% of global greenhouse gas emissions come from the textile industry, according to United Nations estimates. At the same time, many suppliers are located in developing countries that are particularly vulnerable to weather extremes associated with rising temperatures. Suppliers in such markets need access to funds to pay for better machinery and cheaper, renewable energy has eluded to help them adapt.

Emissions are “connected with all of the processes” contained within the fashion industry’s supply chain, García Maceiras said in an interview. “That’s why supporting the transformation of the suppliers — in terms of water consumption, use of chemicals, waste or the implementation of renewable energies — is key.”

The fund’s launch comes as nations gather at the COP31 climate summit in Türkiye to address a US$1.3 trillion goal for climate finance to developing countries. As host country, Türkiye launched the Climate Implementation Bridge in September in order to turn climate commitments into concrete projects.

García Maceiras said that when it comes to textile-related emissions, a collective initiative from the industry is required, in part because suppliers often work with many retailers. As an investor in the fund, Inditex aims to serve as “a catalyst” to bring in other companies, he said.

See also: Vodacom profit jumps 26% as Safaricom gains boost earnings

“This is not an Inditex fund; it’s open to the industry as a whole,” he said. The goal is to “demonstrate that with the involvement of different players within the textile industry, we could reach the objective of the transformation of the whole industry.”

The small and medium-sized suppliers “at the heart of global brand supply chains need access to affordable, appropriately structured financing to stay competitive,” Sarvesh Suri, the IFC’s regional vice president for Asia and the Pacific, said in a statement.

The fund, which will be managed by impact investor Social Investment Managers & Advisors LLC, will help close the climate finance gap by providing loans both to textile makers and to the energy companies they use, according to a joint statement published on Tuesday. Eligible companies may also seek free technical advice on switching to renewable energy sources, to make machinery more energy and water efficient, and reducing chemical use.

See also: Citigroup’s Fraser says China licence gives bank edge on rivals

Other investors in the fund include the US-based Global Environment Facility and the Apparel Impact Institute, the Dutch development bank FMO, French development financier Proparco and British International Investment. The first close is expected to reach $225 million, with more rounds planned to achieve the target goal.

“The success of the fund and the involvement of relevant institutions could open the door for additional, similar initiatives that could reach a wide range of different suppliers,” García Maceiras said.

Inditex’s participation follows more than two years of work at the company to identify the investments suppliers might need to make in order to reduce emissions and other environmental impacts. It’s part of the retailer’s effort to cut its own environmental footprint while maintaining growth.

“The idea is to reduce the total emissions of the group while maintaining the expected growth that we have been achieving consistently year after year,” García Maceiras said. “By 2030, our aim is to reduce up to 53% of our total emissions. At the end of 2025, we reached 11%.”

title: Vodacom profit jumps 26% as Safaricom gains boost earnings
article:
(Nov 10): Vodacom Group Ltd’s half-year headline profit jumped 26% as the company battles to keep control of Safaricom Plc, which boosted the wireless carrier’s earnings during the period.

Vodacom’s so-called headline earnings per share — which exclude one-time gains — climbed to 5.87 rand for the six months ended Sept 30 from 4.67 rand a year earlier.

The firm declared an interim dividend of 3.55 rand, 7.6% higher than a year earlier. Customers increased 12% to a record 250 million.

The Johannesburg-based company that’s majority-owned by the UK’s Vodafone Group Plc, booked a fair-value gain after it remeasured its stake in East Africa’s biggest telecommunications firm.

The increase follows Vodacom’s move to take control of Safaricom after it completed the purchase of an additional 20% interest in June, lifting its effective stake in the Kenyan company to 55%.

That holding is now subject to a legal battle in the country, with the High Court last month declaring the government’s sale of a 15% holding to Vodacom unconstitutional and ordering the shares returned to the state. An appeals court has since allowed Vodacom to retain the shares while fast-tracking an appeal of the ruling.

See also: Citigroup’s Fraser says China licence gives bank edge on rivals

title: TSMC’s revenue rises 60% in a sign of resilient AI chip demand
article:
(Nov 10): Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co posted a 60% increase in monthly sales, reflecting the company’s central role in a global AI infrastructure build-out.

The go-to chipmaker for Nvidia Corp and Apple Inc reported October revenue of NT$586.9 billion. That pace was up from around 51% for the September quarter. Analysts on average are projecting 63% growth for the year’s final three months.

Taiwan’s largest company last month delivered a better-than-expected revenue outlook, sustaining a torrid pace of growth in the post-ChatGPT era. Yet investors continue to grapple with the longer-term outlook for AI demand, given the rising cost of financing expensive and resource-hungry data centres. TSMC’s shares have gyrated alongside the rest of the tech sector, buffeted by fears that the Democrats’ sweep of Congress in the US midterms may lead to tougher oversight of the artificial intelligence sector.

TSMC — a key barometer for the industry because it makes chips for a broad swathe of tech players — is betting on a fundamental shift. It is trying to build and furnish about 20 factories at home and overseas, an unprecedented pace for a company that typically works on four or five new buildings simultaneously.

CEO C C Wei has stressed, though, that it remains in prudent expansion mode, exploring a new manufacturing site in Texas while discussing a potential tie-up with Elon Musk’s Terafab chipmaking endeavour.

See also: Japan’s Rapidus is said likely to miss mass production deadline

The company has so far managed to accelerate sales growth and ramped up capacity expansion. The company reiterated its capital expenditures will reach as much as US$64 billion, a record, this year.

title: Rising fuel flows through Hormuz may help ease strained market
article:
(Nov 10): The volume of refined products being loaded within the Persian Gulf is rising, with most of that exiting the Strait of Hormuz and providing some relief to one of the tightest corners of the global oil market nine months into the Iran war.

The region loaded about three million barrels a day of distillates, including diesel, petrochemical feedstock naphtha and liquefied petroleum gas, in October, according to data from ship-tracking and analytics firm Vortexa Ltd. While that is still only about half of pre-conflict levels, that is up from a trough in May of about one million barrels a day.

Most of those shipments have or will soon exit through Hormuz, said Xavier Tang, senior market analyst for Vortexa, although exact volumes are hard to pin down due to transfers within the Gulf and methods of obfuscating flows such as vessels turning off their transponders. Still, the recovery in oil products is lagging that for crude, which at some points in prior months had neared early-February levels.

“Crude is going at about 80% to 85% of pre-war levels” including pipeline exports, while “products are at about 35% to 40%,” Fereidun Fesharaki, chairman emeritus of industry consultant FGE NexantECA, said last week, referring to Middle Eastern oil exports including through Hormuz.

There’s been an overall pickup in vessel traffic across different commodities in the crucial waterway. Crude remains the most successful at exiting the embattled region, while flows of liquefied natural gas have risen to about a third of levels before the conflict.

See also: Oil extends drop as Trump says further Iran strikes unnecessary

“Oil infrastructure such as refineries remains susceptible to drone strikes,” which has led the region’s producers to prioritise crude shipments, Tang said.

Global refined markets remain tight, with some countries opting to prioritise local consumption despite attractive profits on exports. International shipments of diesel from major producer China, for example, may remain curbed as the country grapples with low domestic inventories.

title: Copper extends rebound as global technology stocks resume rally
article:
(Nov 10): Copper extended its rebound from last week’s slump, tracking a rally in technology shares due to the metal’s use in power infrastructure and data centres.

The industrial metal has moved in tandem with artificial intelligence stocks in recent months. It had slumped 2.7% to a three-month low last week as concerns rose that the Democrats’ sweep of US midterm elections could mean greater regulation of AI.

Stocks advanced on Tuesday (Nov 10), with South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi Index the top performer in the region. In China, the market was hit by a supply squeeze that’s driving a rapid surge in spot premiums to record levels.

The tightness has started to bring in more imported cargoes as traders aim to take advantage of an arbitrage window to bring in metal from overseas at a profit, Jinrui Futures Co said in a note.

Investors were also monitoring a major shortage in the global aluminium market fuelled by declining stockpiles of the crucial industrial commodity. Buyers are facing rising prices for spot metal and there is little immediate prospect of relief before new shipments from Indonesia arrive.

Copper rose 0.3% to US$13,937 a tonne on the London Metal Exchange as of 10.52am in Shanghai. Aluminium slipped 0.3% to US$3,058.50 while other metals edged higher. Iron ore was down 0.2% at US$92.55 a tonne in Singapore.

See also: Asian rice price climbs near two-year high in inflation threat

title: Japan’s Rapidus is said likely to miss mass production deadline
article:
(Nov 10): Japanese government-backed startup Rapidus Corp has fallen behind schedule on its high-stakes pledge to mass produce cutting-edge chips by March 2028 and may no longer be able to make that deadline.

The startup, which has received billions of dollars’ worth of public funds, has yet to successfully produce a key type of advanced memory that is an essential component of all processors, people familiar with the matter said. Rapidus has yet to produce functioning static random access memory cells, or SRAM, a critical step that needed to be completed by the summer to manufacture 2nm chips in time, they said.

Engineers are under intense pressure to pick up the pace but the failure to meet that technological milestone means the company is at least months behind schedule, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public.

A significant delay may jeopardise public support for Rapidus, widely viewed as a long-shot attempt to build a top-tier foundry from scratch and lower Japan’s advanced chip reliance on Taiwan, which China claims as its own. Dust and particle control within the cleanroom remains another issue the company is working to resolve, the people said.

The government has so far officially earmarked more than ¥2 trillion in state funding to Rapidus. Severe technological issues could also push back Rapidus’s goal of going public by 2032.

“Rapidus continues to devote its full efforts toward the start of mass production in the second half of fiscal 2027,” a spokesperson said in an email. The company declined to provide details about its technological development, which it said is confidential. In September, a panel of outside experts commissioned by a government agency reported the company’s development is progressing, it said.

See also: TSMC said to mull making advanced AI memory chips

Last month, Rapidus chairman Tetsuro Higashi said the venture was on track for mass production as scheduled, without elaborating.

Advanced logic chips require hundreds of millions of embedded SRAM cells. Manufacturers need to reproduce each of these cells, including their transistors, at atomic-scale precision to prevent operational failures and ensure stable data retention. At the nanometre scale, even a minor microscopic deviation can cause debilitating chip failures.

Rapidus will continue to pursue 2nm manufacturing and may ultimately succeed after some years’ delay, the people said. Rapidus seeks to compete against Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, which is building facilities in the US, Intel Corp and Samsung Electronics Co. All are racing to develop manufacturing processes and meet artificial intelligence service providers’ voracious demand for increasingly powerful chips.

See also: OpenAI’s Altman meets Samsung executives as chip crunch deepens

After launching its pilot production line at its factory in Hokkaido, northern Japan, Rapidus said in July last year that it successfully manufactured functioning transistors — an early step toward making cutting-edge chips. Since then, technological progress has consisted mainly of process design kit releases.

Last month, Economy Minister Ryosei Akazawa said the government was ready to continue supporting Rapidus until the venture becomes financially viable, given the importance of cutting-edge chips for Japan’s economic security. Since Rapidus’ creation in 2022, TSMC has built a plant in southern Japan, with plans to build another factory that will manufacture 3nm chips.

In September, independent director Yoshimitsu Kobayashi told Bloomberg News that Rapidus is targeting mass production with a yield of at least 80%, or four out of every five chips produced. CEO Atsuyoshi Koike, who has floated plans to build two additional factories in Hokkaido and a plant on the moon, and representative director Atsuo Shimizu have said that Kobayashi’s definition is not shared by all executives.

title: Citigroup’s Fraser says China licence gives bank edge on rivals
article:
(Nov 10): Citigroup Inc chief executive officer Jane Fraser said a securities licence in China completes the bank’s product offering there and gives it an edge over competitors.

“All I would say to the competition is watch out, because we have this unique offering already from that global network, the history we’ve got, and now with this,” Fraser said to Bloomberg Television in Shanghai.

After a five-year wait, the lender last month received a approval for the licence to run a securities business in mainland China, far later than many of its competitors.

The firm’s path has been fraught with delays. Since applying in late 2021, the bank has had to navigate shifting Chinese data-security rules and scrutiny from US regulators.

The license lets the bank raise capital, trade and get better access to investors, Fraser said. It also lets Citigroup connect investors between the world and China, she said.

Kaleem Rizvi, global co-head of corporate banking, said in an interview from Shanghai that the firm envisions hiring about 100 bankers over the next several years after it won approval for the licence.

See also: European Investment Bank’s Calvino says US turmoil is driving capital to Europe

As for the AI market, Fraser said that last week’s selloff was a tad overdone, with hedge funds taking money off the table. She said the need for compute is not going away and called the AI buildout a multiyear effort, though not everyone will be a winner.

“When you have innovation at that speed, you need to have risk management at that speed,” Fraser said.

Citigroup reported a record third quarter, Fraser said, with growth across its business lines.

See also: BMW widens battery component suppliers with Samsung, LG Energy

For 2027, she said the aim is to diversify the businesses for all seasons so the bank can support clients as they transform and grow. She said she would love a year a little more boring than 2026.

title: Singapore extends GST waiver to activities related to wholesale gold transactions
article:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and Ministry of Finance (MOF) will be extending the GST waiver to specified wholesale investment precious metal (IPM) related services between institutional participants covered by the existing GST framework. These services include activities such as vaulting, refining, recasting, assaying, and broking.

The initiative seeks to support the growth of wholesale Loco Singapore gold market activities where the gold traded is not for domestic consumption. This enhanced tax framework is expected to take effect from April 2027, with further details to be announced at Budget 2027.

Under the current Approved Refiner and Consolidator Scheme, GST is waived on IPM-related goods supplied between approved refiners and consolidators for refining activities, to ease their cashflow and compliance.The existing framework also exempts the import and local supply of IPM from GST.

Deputy prime minister and MAS chairman Gan Kim Yong thinks the enhanced GST framework will both facilitate the trading of gold and central bank storage of gold in Singapore. He adds: “I have to emphasise that this is a transaction between institutions and the wholesale trade, and it's not targeted at the consumer retail market. So that is why the GST framework is built on that basis.”

Speaking at a media doorstop, Gan also announced that MAS is launching its central bank gold vaulting service. “Given an increasingly uncertain external environment, demand for gold as an asset class is rising as investors and central banks look for resilience and diversification,” says Gan. “Foreign central banks and sovereign entities now have an additional sovereign custody option in Singapore for their gold reserves.”

Besides offering an alternative storage option, the service also provides secure, allocated custody, reliable servicing and efficient access to gold-market liquidity during Asian trading hours, notes MAS.

See also: Central banks buy gold at fastest pace since 2024, WGC says

Under this development, MAS will store up to 500 tonnes of gold in its national currency vault, with room for expansion as demand grows. MAS will also offer gold custody accounts to select Singapore-based bullion banks with expertise and experience in providing gold-related services and trading liquidity to these institutions.

Gan says that the development of Singapore’s gold market is a “natural extension” to Singapore’s role as a trusted financial centre and will anchor new high-value activities across trading, risk management, custody, and professional services in the city-state.

“By connecting secure storage with trading and settlement, we are building a market where gold can be held, managed and traded in Singapore,” he adds. “It will create good jobs and capabilities, while adding depth and resilience to our financial sector, strengthening Singapore’s role as a trusted connector between Asia and global gold markets.”

See also: Gold climbs back from one-year low as dip buyers arrest slide

Gan also shared that Singapore’s gold clearing system will be ready by end-2026, with live trading and liquidity building up from the first quarter next year. In June, DBS, Deutsche Bank, ICBC Standard Bank, JP Morgan, OCBC, and UOB signed a memorandum of understanding with SGX Group to develop an over-the-counter gold clearing system,

MAS announced that industry testing of the clearing system has been completed and the clearing system rulebook will be finalised soon. Live trading and market operations are expected to commence in 1Q 2027, with gold market liquidity building throughout the year.

JP Morgan senior country officer Wai Mei Hong says, “We are pleased to work with SGX Group in advancing Singapore’s OTC gold clearing system. As global demand for gold grows, this initiative will strengthen Singapore’s role as a trading hub, deepen liquidity across time zones and help us better serve clients.”

UOB head of group global markets Kelvin Ng says that the combination of vaulting, enhanced tax support for wholesale gold activities and a gold clearing ecosystem will create "stronger foundations" for market growth. “These developments will deepen liquidity, improve price discovery and reinforce Singapore's role as a key precious metals centre serving the Asia-Pacific region,” adds Ng.

In addition, it was also announced that SGX is targeting to launch its physically deliverable gold kilobar futures in the second quarter of 2027.
